title: Njord: A Probabilistic Graph Neural Network for Ensemble Ocean Forecasting
claim: A latent-variable graph network encodes state and forcing to a mesh, processes it with sampled noise, and decodes a residual-added stochastic prediction.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right, globe graphs with encode/decode trapezoid insets and skip arrow
description: A left-to-right pipeline built on three large globe renderings. On the left, a globe covered with orange mesh nodes and blue edges shows the encoded graph. A trapezoid inset labeled 'Encode to graph' links stacked ocean-state maps (States X^{t-2:t-1}) and forcing maps (Forcing F^{t-2:t}) to the mesh through a brace. A thick arrow leads to the center, a dense orange mesh labeled 'GNN Processor'. Above it, a boxed inset shows hierarchical graph layers, with a black arrow bringing in the latent variable Z^t ~ N(μ, I). Another thick arrow leads to the right-hand globe, with a 'Decode to grid' trapezoid inset. A dashed arrow labeled X^{t-1} runs along the bottom to the output ocean maps, labeled X̂^t ~ p̂_θ. Orange, blue and black dominate, and the eye goes first to the globes.
caption: One-step prediction in the Njord model. Residuals are predicted at time t, which are then added to the previous state Xt−1 in order to produce the sample ˆXt. The corresponding overview of Njord-Baltic is shown in Figure 11 in the appendix.
abstract: Ocean dynamics are inherently chaotic, yet existing machine learning ocean models produce only deterministic forecasts. We introduce Njord, a probabilistic data-driven model for ocean forecasting, applicable to both global and regional domains. Njord combines a deep latent variable framework with a graph neural network architecture, enabling sampling each forecast step in a single forward pass. We apply Njord globally at 0.25Â° resolution and regionally to the Baltic Sea at 2 km resolution. To scale to these large ocean grids we introduce K-means cluster meshes that adapt to irregular sea surface geometry. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both domains compared to deterministic machine learning baselines, while also providing uncertainty estimates from the sampled ensemble forecasts. On the global OceanBench benchmark, Njord achieves the lowest errors on average across upper-ocean variables when evaluated against real-world observations, with the largest improvements in surface temperature prediction.
